lesson_title: Blazers, Badges and Receipts: Quadrilaterals and Their Proofs
hook_text: Every square is a rectangle. Almost no rectangle is a square. That one sentence is the trap.
clip_script: Quadrilaterals are one family, and every child inherits everything its parent had, then adds one thing. The grandparent is just four sides. The parallelogram adds one rule: both pairs of opposite sides run parallel, like two rails and two sleepers. The rectangle adds square corners. The rhombus adds four equal sides. And the square is the youngest, inheriting from both. Here is the trap. It works like a school uniform: everyone wears the blazer, but only prefects wear the badge. Seeing a badge tells you the person is in the school. Seeing the blazer tells you nothing about prefecthood. So every square is a rectangle, and plenty of rectangles are not squares. Inheritance runs downward only. Now the geometry-writing rule, in one picture: proving a phone is yours by saying 'it's mine' convinces nobody — you show the till slip. Every line of a proof is a claim, and every claim needs its receipt written next to it. A true statement with no reason scores zero. And you cannot use the receipt for something you have not yet proved you own — never use a parallelogram's properties until you have shown the shape IS one.
visual_style: A family tree of shapes lighting up one inheritance at a time; a blazer with a badge pinning on; a till slip printing beside each line of a proof.
pacing: Steady down the family tree, a sharp beat on the badge, deliberate on the receipts.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write proofs that actually collect their marks.
